newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African parliament approves Namibian debt deal.
newsitem.headline: S.African parliament approves Namibian debt deal.

text.p: South Africa's parliament on Friday approved legislation that would result in South Africa assuming 1.2 billion rand in debt and interest payments owed by Namibia.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel told the national assembly the Exchequer Amendment Bill signalled a new era in regional relations even though it would add 1.2 billion rand to South Africa's debt burden.
The National Party opposed the move saying it would make South Africa one of the largest donors of development aid in the world.
President Nelson Mandela signed an agreement with Namibia's President Sam Nujoma in 1994 to take over the debt incurred while Namibia was under South African control.
Manuel said the two countries agreed that the loan would be redeemed by Namibia over 20 years, starting with a capital repayment grace period of three years.

"Although the government of Namibia agreed to a debt settlement proposal in 1992, it has always maintained that the government of Namibia could not be expected to assume responsibility for its colonial debts," Manuel said.

Manual said the South African government would take over 12 Namibian bond issue series outstanding in the South African capital market totalling 268.5 million rand, and a South African Reserve Bank facility to Namibia totalling 842.8 million rand.
"Government debt will therefore be increased by an amount of about 1.1 billion rand on the debt takeover date," Manuel said.

"Interest to maturity on the bond in the market amounts to 131.4 million rand. The total financial obligation that will be transferred to the South African government therefore amounts to 1.2 billion rand," he added.
The date of the debt takeover would be announced once a bilateral agreement on the issue had been signed.
African National Congress legislator Rob Davies said the debt could have been a major source of potential contestation between the two countries.
"It (Namibia) would have had to repay 78 million rand over seven years beginning in 1995," he said.
"This was equivalent to 2.3 percent of Namibia's export earnings or 9.6 percent of the country's gross domestic fixed investment," he added
The National Party opposed the bill on a matter of principle because it claimed that Namibia had been highly subsidised by South African taxpayers.
It also said Namibia had a "very favourable debt rate of 16 percent of GDP, which was four times better than South Africa's.
